title: Two reviewers, two scores
scenario: Lantern Studio is writing the rubric it will use to compare two image models for Fernhill Candles. You judge the rubric and how the scores are combined, using the exhibit. The rubric, the scores and the pass line are made up for this case.
exhibit:
RUBRIC DRAFT 1 (made up for this case)
  Mood: rate the mood from 1 to 5.

SCORES, MOOD LINE (made up)
  Image 7    Reviewer A: 5    Reviewer B: 2
  Image 12   Reviewer A: 4    Reviewer B: 4
  Image 19   Reviewer A: 2    Reviewer B: 5

APPROVED WORK (made up)
  The art director has approved 3 past images: AD-1, AD-2, AD-3.
  No written rubric exists for them.

SCORECARD RULE (made up)
  Four lines, each scored 1 to 5, then averaged.
  Pass line: a mean of 4.0 or more.

IMAGE 31 (made up)
  Brief fit 5    Brand 5    Label text 5    Logo 1
  Mean = (5 + 5 + 5 + 1) / 4 = 4.0   ->  PASS

JOB TYPES (made up)
  Packshots: exact product, exact label, plain background.
  Social stories: mood, safe zone at the top for text, vertical 9:16.

questions.prompt: Reviewers A and B differ by three points on images 7 and 19. What should you add to the mood line first?

options.text: A sample image pinned to each scale level, so both reviewers compare to the same picture
options.explanation: Right. OpenAI's "show rather than tell" advice is to give examples of different score levels.

options.text: A longer scale from 1 to 100, so that small differences between two images show up
options.explanation: A longer scale gives more room to disagree. It does not tell reviewers what a 3 looks like.

options.text: A rule that the more senior reviewer's score always replaces the other one on any image
options.explanation: This hides the disagreement. The rubric stays unclear for the next reviewer.

options.text: A note saying that reviewers should try harder to agree, and should talk less during scoring
options.explanation: Effort does not fix a vague line. The scale needs examples.

questions.prompt: There is no written rubric, only the three approved images. What is the best way to start?

options.text: Write a rubric of 40 lines alone, from memory, and test it after both models have run
options.explanation: That is slow, and it skips testing the rubric on people before the real run.

options.text: Ask a model to write a rubric from the words "good candle photo" and use it as it is
options.explanation: A rubric made from three words has nothing real to hold on to, and it was never checked by a person.

options.text: Show a model the approved images, ask why they work, then edit its list and test it
options.explanation: Right. Claude's outcomes docs suggest starting from a known-good example, and the draft still needs a person's edit and test.

options.text: Skip the rubric, since approved images prove the studio already knows what good means
options.explanation: The studio's taste is in the images, but the reviewers need it written as lines they can apply.

questions.prompt: Image 31 has the wrong logo, yet the scorecard says PASS. What is the best fix?

options.text: Raise the pass line to 4.5, so one low line can no longer be absorbed by the others
options.explanation: A higher line still lets an average hide a weak must-have: 5, 5, 5 and 3 gives a mean of 4.5.

options.text: Keep the rule, because the mean is the fairest way to combine four very different lines
options.explanation: The mean let an image with a wrong logo pass. A client would reject it.

options.text: Remove the logo line, since it is the one that pulls the average down for the new model here
options.explanation: Removing a must-have line to raise scores makes the test less honest.

options.text: Make logo and label text must-pass gates, and score brief fit and brand as weights
options.explanation: Right. The Anthropic engineering post describes binary, weighted and hybrid scoring. A hybrid keeps must-haves as gates.

questions.prompt: Even with sample images, the two reviewers still differ by two points or more on 3 of 20 images. What do you do?

options.text: Remove those 3 images from the set, because they cannot be scored in any fair way at all
options.explanation: Hard images are exactly the cases a test set needs. Removing them hides the problem.

options.text: Average the two scores on those 3 images and then move on to the next batch of work
options.explanation: An average of 2 and 5 hides that the rubric was unclear.

options.text: Look at the 3 images together, fix the wording, then score a fresh set in another round
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs recommend multiple rounds of detailed human review to refine the scorecard.

options.text: Keep both scores for every image and let the client choose which reviewer to trust more
options.explanation: The client should not have to settle a gap in the studio's own rubric.

questions.prompt: The studio wants the same rubric for packshots and for social stories. What do you advise?

options.text: Use one long rubric for both, and let reviewers skip any line they feel does not apply
options.explanation: Skipped lines mean two reviewers may score different things. The result is not comparable.

options.text: Write one rubric for each job type, since each type has different must-have lines
options.explanation: Right. Claude's guide says a use case may need several rubrics for holistic evaluation.

options.text: Use the packshot rubric for both, because packshots are the harder job of the two
options.explanation: A packshot rubric has no line for mood or a safe zone, which social stories need.

options.text: Use one short rubric of three lines, so that it stays fair for every kind of job
options.explanation: Three general lines cannot hold an exact-label gate and a safe-zone line at once.
